title: Data Security: Encryption, Cloud KMS / CMEK, and Secret Manager
bodyMarkdown:
## Encryption at rest is already on

Google Cloud encrypts customer content at rest by default with **AES-256** (the [default encryption documentation](https://cloud.google.com/docs/security/encryption/default-encryption) notes a small number of legacy Persistent Disks created before 2015 use AES-128). No configuration, no extra cost, and no performance decision is needed. Data is split into chunks; each chunk gets its own **data encryption key (DEK)**, and when a chunk is updated it is encrypted with a new key. DEKs are wrapped by **key encryption keys (KEKs)** held in Google's internal Keystore, which are not exportable. This is **envelope encryption**, and Cloud KMS uses the same pattern for CMEK.

So the architect's question is never "is it encrypted?" but **"who controls the key, and what is the revocation story?"**

## Choosing a key-management model

| Model | Key custody | Your revocation lever | Trade-offs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Google-managed (default)** | Google | None | Free, zero operations, shared across customers, no per-customer key audit trail |
| **CMEK** (Cloud KMS) | You own the key; Google services use it on your behalf | Revoke the service agent's role, disable the key, or destroy it | Cloud KMS cost scales with key versions and cryptographic operations; wide service support; you can audit every use |
| **CMEK with Cloud HSM** | Key lives in FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs | Same as CMEK | Higher cost than software keys; no HSM-specific code needed |
| **CMEK with Cloud EKM** | Key stays in an external partner system | Cut off the external key | Google cannot access your key material, but if the external system is unavailable your data is too |
| **CSEK** (customer-supplied) | You supply a 256-bit key with each use; Google does not store it | Stop supplying the key | Narrow support, heavy client burden, and **deprecated for Compute Engine** |

The [CMEK documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/cmek) frames the benefits as ownership, auditability, and logical separation of data through encryption. It also carries a warning that matters in design reviews: if the CMEK is disabled or destroyed, or the service agent loses its role, the data cannot be accessed, and some services can suffer **permanent data loss** if the key stays inaccessible too long.

**Decision rule:**
- No regulatory or contractual key-control requirement: stay with default encryption.
- Need to control rotation, prove key usage in audit logs, or have a kill switch, without running your own hardware: **CMEK in Cloud KMS**.
- Policy demands FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware: **CMEK with Cloud HSM** protection.
- Key material must live outside Google, for example under a separate custodian: **Cloud EKM**.
- Need to supply raw key material yourself: CSEK, but check current support first, because the CSEK page for Compute Engine marks it deprecated and recommends Cloud KMS keys.

## Cloud KMS essentials

**Resource model.** A **key ring** contains **keys**; a key contains **key versions** that hold the actual material. Per the [Cloud KMS resources documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/resource-hierarchy), a key ring **cannot be deleted** after creation, KMS resources cannot be moved to another location, a key's purpose cannot change after creation, and deleted key names cannot be reused. Choose locations carefully: the CMEK guidance recommends creating the key ring geographically near the resources it protects.

**Protection levels.** Per the [protection levels page](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/protection-levels): software keys use the BoringCrypto module (FIPS 140-3 Level 1); multi-tenant Cloud HSM uses FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSMs and can provide attestation; single-tenant HSM gives dedicated partitions and is regional only; Cloud EKM comes in internet and VPC flavors. EKM over the internet is unavailable in the `nam-eur-asia1` and `global` locations, and EKM over VPC is not available in multi-region locations.

**Key version states.** The [key states documentation](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/key-states) matters for revocation and recovery:

| State | Usable? | Reversible? |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Yes | n/a |
| Disabled | No, but material retained | Yes, re-enable |
| Scheduled for destruction | No | Yes, restore to disabled within the window |
| Destroyed | No, material gone | No (apart from re-importing previously imported keys) |

The default scheduled-destruction window is **30 days**; it can be set from **24 hours to 120 days** at key creation and cannot be changed afterwards. Destroyed material takes 45 days to be fully deleted from Google systems. Practical implication: **disable first** when you want an emergency, reversible kill switch; destroy only when you are sure.

**Rotation.** The [key rotation guidance](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/key-rotation) recommends automatic rotation on a regular schedule, with 90 days as an illustrative period. Three facts trip people up: rotation does **not** re-encrypt existing data, old versions stay active (and keep incurring cost) until destroyed so legacy data remains decryptable, and Cloud KMS does **not** auto-rotate asymmetric keys.

**Separation of duties.** The [separation of duties guidance](https://cloud.google.com/kms/docs/separation-of-duties) distinguishes **key managers** (Cloud KMS Admin: create, rotate, change state, delete) from **key users** (CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter: use the key). Admins should not be able to decrypt data they have no reason to read. Regulated organizations are advised to keep keys in a **dedicated key project**; if keys sit in the same project as the data, use IAM deny policies to strip encrypt/decrypt permissions from key managers. **Autokey** automates CMEK provisioning and grants the usage role to the **service agent** rather than to the human requesting the key, so IaC pipelines do not need elevated privileges.

Grant `roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter` only to the specific service agents that must use each key, ideally per key rather than per project.

## Secret Manager

Use Secret Manager for API keys, passwords, tokens, and certificates, never baked into images, environment files in repos, or chat. Per the [overview](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/overview), each secret holds **versions** (disable, destroy with optional delayed destruction, alias, roll back), supports **automatic rotation schedules**, encrypts in transit with TLS and at rest with AES-256, and can use CMEK. **Replication** is automatic (Google picks regions, billed as one location) or user-managed (you choose regions, billed per location).

The [best practices page](https://cloud.google.com/secret-manager/docs/best-practices) gives the operational rules:

- **Least privilege at secret level:** bind `roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor` on the specific secret, not the whole project, when several services share a project. IAM Conditions and the IAM recommender help trim access.
- **Pin versions** in production. The documentation recommends referencing a version number rather than `latest`, so a bad rotation cannot silently break or compromise a running service; `latest` is convenient but makes rollouts implicit.
- **Rotate regularly** and keep apps able to pick up the new version without a redeploy.
- **Prefer API access over mounting secrets in the file system or environment variables**, because file-system exposure raises the severity of traversal bugs.
- **Disable before destroying**, so deletion is reversible.
- **Avoid expiry on production secrets**; use time-based IAM conditions instead.
- **Enable Data Access audit logs** at folder or org level, put secrets inside a **VPC Service Controls perimeter**, and use regional secrets when residency is strict.
- **Do not export service account keys** to reach Secret Manager: use attached service accounts, Workload Identity for GKE, or Workload Identity Federation off-cloud.

## Compliance connection

CMEK plus Data Access audit logging gives demonstrable control of keys and an access record. Cloud KMS and Secret Manager are among the products covered by Google's HIPAA BAA (see the [HIPAA documentation](https://cloud.google.com/security/compliance/hipaa)), but the BAA does not configure anything for you: you still choose CMEK, logging, and least-privilege IAM. A related PHI rule: do not put PHI into resource metadata or monitoring labels.

## Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- **Believing default encryption is "not enough" for compliance** without a stated key-control requirement. Default is strong; CMEK adds control, not stronger ciphers.
- **Destroying a key to "pause" access.** Disable instead; destruction is the irreversible end of a lifecycle.
- **One person who is both Cloud KMS Admin and Encrypter/Decrypter.**
- **Granting `secretAccessor` or `secretmanager.admin` at project level** to every workload.
- **Assuming rotation fixes old data.** Existing data stays under the old key version until rewritten.
- **Choosing CSEK for convenience.** A lost customer-supplied key means unrecoverable data; Google cannot help.
- **Key ring in the wrong location**, which cannot be fixed later because KMS resources cannot be moved.
- **Service account key JSON in repos**, shared passphrases, or secrets in environment variables everywhere.

## Exam tips

- **Default is encrypted:** every byte at rest is AES-256 encrypted with Google-managed keys; the exam question is about key control, not whether encryption exists.
- **CMEK is the default answer for key control:** kill switch by disabling or destroying the key, no hardware to run; Cloud HSM for FIPS 140-2 Level 3, Cloud EKM for keys held outside Google.
- **CSEK means you hold the key:** lose it and the data is unrecoverable; it is a narrow, deprecated-for-Compute-Engine option, rarely the best answer.
- **Disable before destroy:** disabled is reversible, scheduled destruction defaults to 30 days and is restorable within the window, destroyed is final.
- **Rotation does not re-encrypt:** old versions remain usable for decryption; asymmetric keys are not auto-rotated.
- **Separate key admins from key users:** Cloud KMS Admin versus CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter granted to the service agent, ideally with keys in a dedicated project.
- **Secret Manager over code and env files:** grant `secretAccessor` on the specific secret, pin versions in production, rotate, and enable Data Access logs.
- **Compliance link:** CMEK plus Data Access logs support HIPAA and PCI evidence, but the customer still configures them.

flowchart TD
  App["Application writes data"] --> Svc["Cloud Storage or BigQuery"]
  Svc -- "service agent uses key" --> KMS["Cloud KMS key (CMEK)"]
  KMS --> Enc["Data encrypted at rest"]
  Admin["Key admin"] --> Disable["Disable key or revoke service agent role"]
  Disable --> KMS
  Disable --> Lost["Data inaccessible until key restored"]
